german: This is what gets cooked between the North Sea and the Alps, from Spinatknödel (spinach dumplings) and Handkäs mit Musik to Streuselkuchen baked on a tray. You can also put up preserves like pumpkin and orange, or make Quarkkeulchen in the air fryer.
japanese: Ramen is only the start, even if Tori-Chintan, a clear chicken broth, is the base for many bowls. You will also find Kitsune-Udon with sweet tofu, chilled Hiyayakko and Ochazuke, rice with hot tea poured over it.
irish: Irish cooking runs on potatoes, oats, buttermilk and whatever the sea brings in. Make yourself Champ, a Seafood Chowder or Corned Beef and Cabbage, and bake a Brown Soda Bread on the side, which needs no yeast at all.
kurdish: Bulgur, yoghurt, sumac and lamb carry this kitchen, and you taste them in many of the dishes. Try Kufteya somaq, meatballs with sumac, the yoghurt soup Dokliw, or finish with Zerde, a saffron rice pudding.
portuguese: Salt cod, beans, sausage and plenty of olive oil sit at the centre of many of these dishes. Make Bacalhau à Brás with matchstick potatoes and egg, braise Favas com chouriço, or bake Broa de milho, a cornbread with a little rye.
mediterranean: Here you cook with vegetables, pulses, olive oil and herbs, the way people eat around the Mediterranean. Blend a hummus, braise a Caponata, make Muhammara from peppers and walnuts, or bake a rosemary focaccia.
asian: From miso soup with tofu to Mapo Tofu with Sichuan pepper, this collection crosses several Asian kitchens. For a quick evening there is beef with broccoli, filled Onigiri or a wonton soup.
italian: Ripe tomatoes, day-old bread and a piece of Parmesan are often all this kitchen needs. Make Spaghetti al Pomodoro, a Parmigiana di Melanzane, Polpette in tomato sauce, or Ribollita, the Tuscan bread and bean stew.
baden-wuerttemberg: Between Swabia and Baden a lot of the cooking is done with dough, as Maultaschen, Schupfnudeln and Krautspätzle show. Add to that onion tart, Bibbeleskäs from Baden and, for something sweet, an Ofenschlupfer bread pudding.
bayern: A proper Brotzeit with radish and sausage salad belongs here just as much as Backhendl, fried chicken, on Sunday. Franconia brings Elisenlebkuchen and Rothenburger Schneeballen, the Allgäu its cheese soup.
berlin: Berlin eats hearty food without fuss, from currywurst to Eisbein (pork knuckle) with sauerkraut and pea purée. With coffee there are Berliner Pfannkuchen, in the pub pickled eggs and rollmops, and in summer a Berliner Weiße mit Schuss.
brandenburg: The Spree, the Havel and countless lakes supply pike-perch and crayfish for this region's cooking. The Spreewald brings braised cucumbers and quark with linseed oil, Lusatia its Plinsen pancakes and poppy seed cake with crumble.
hamburg: In the port city a lot of fish ends up on the plate, as Pannfisch, Finkenwerder plaice or a fish roll with Bismarck herring. Pears, beans and bacon belong here too, and in the morning a Franzbrötchen cinnamon pastry.
hessen: Grüne Soße with its seven herbs is Frankfurt's calling card, and here you get it with schnitzel too. Drink a spritzed apple wine with it, and with coffee there are Bethmännchen or Frankfurter Brenten made from marzipan.
mecklenburg-vorpommern: On the Baltic coast herring and plaice come first, as fried herring or as May plaice with fried potatoes. Sea buckthorn joins in as a cream or hot in a glass, and on holidays there is Mecklenburg roast goose with dried fruit.
niedersachsen: The coast gives you Cuxhaven shrimp soup and East Frisian Snirtjebraten, the heath its Heidschnucke lamb roast. With tea you bake Heidesand shortbread or thin East Frisian New Year wafers.
nordrhein-westfalen: Between Münsterland, the Rhineland and Lippe the cooking is down to earth and filling. Here you will find broad beans with bacon, Lippischer Pickert, Rhenish Döppekooche (potato bake) and Bergische Waffeln with hot cherries.
rheinland-pfalz: Wine goes into many pots here, into trout in Riesling sauce as much as into the wine custard. The Palatinate brings Saumagen, liver dumplings with sauerkraut and chestnut soup, and Kirschenmichel cherry pudding for dessert.
sachsen: Saxony loves to bake, as you can see from Dresdner Eierschecke, Christstollen and Pulsnitz gingerbread. The savoury side brings Leipziger Allerlei, Karpfen blau (poached carp) and Saxon goose giblets with prunes.
schleswig-holstein: Between the North Sea and the Baltic, shrimp, mussels and fish soup come to the table. Add Dithmarscher Mehlbeutel, Holstein cabbage pudding, Grüne Grütze with vanilla sauce and, on cold evenings, a grog.
kanto: Around Tokyo people eat fast and hearty, whether Gyudon on rice, tempura or Monjayaki, the runny cabbage pancake. Napolitan, spaghetti with ketchup, comes from Yokohama, and for sushi there are Nigiri and Chirashi-Zushi.
kansai: Osaka gives you Takoyaki, Kushikatsu and Battera, the pressed mackerel sushi. Kyoto adds a rich Kotteri ramen, and to finish there are Mitarashi Dango, rice dumplings with a sweet soy glaze.
kyushu: In the south of Japan you make ramen with a rich pork bone broth, above all Hakata-style Tonkotsu. Nagasaki brings Champon, Kakuni-Don with braised pork belly, and Kasutera, the sponge cake with Portuguese roots.
chubu: Nagoya cooks bold flavours, with red miso broth in Miso-Nikomi-Udon and crisp chicken wings called Tebasaki. Yamanashi brings Hoto, a noodle stew with pumpkin, and for breakfast there is Ogura Toast with sweet bean paste.
hokkaido: In Japan's cold north, seafood and butter take centre stage, in Hotate Bata-yaki as much as in Chanchan-yaki with salmon and miso. Sapporo adds miso ramen and Soup Curry, and Jingisukan is lamb from the tabletop grill.
tohoku: In Japan's northeast you find ramen with red miso from Sendai, with anchovy dashi from Tsugaru, or ice cold from Yamagata. Alongside there is Kiritanpo-Nabe with rice sticks, grilled beef tongue and Zunda Mochi.
chugoku: Hiroshima is known for its oysters, and here you get them breaded as Kaki Fry, in ramen or in the miso hotpot Dote-Nabe. There is also okonomiyaki, which Hiroshima layers and fries with yakisoba noodles.
ulster: In Ulster the cooking relies on oats, potatoes, treacle and fresh fish. Here you get Pratie Oaten from the pan, Treacle Scones, Cockelty Pie with cockles and Yellowman, the honeycomb toffee from Ballycastle.
munster: In the south of Ireland Cashel Blue cheese turns up often, in a leek tart, in a salad with pear or as a butter for steak. Add Kerry Pies with lamb, Limerick Ham cooked in cider and Bastible Bread, baked in a pot.
connacht: In the west of Ireland much comes from sea and river, fried oysters for one or trout in an oatmeal crust. From the land come Boxty made of raw and mashed potato, and Carrageen Moss Pudding, set with seaweed.
dublin: Dublin likes its fish in batter with thick chips, as Smoked Cod or Ray and Chips. It gets fancier with Dublin Lawyer, lobster in whiskey cream, and with tea there is Gur Cake, the Dublin fruit slice.
leinster: In the east of Ireland, from Wicklow to Wexford, you cook with game, fish and fruit from the garden. Try venison stew with stout, haddock in mustard cream, Wexford Rissoles and, for dessert, strawberries with cream and meringue.
lisboa: Lisbon and Sintra bring Bifana and Prego no pão, both served in a roll, clams à Bulhão Pato and grilled sardines. With coffee you have a Pastel de nata or a Travesseiro from Sintra with almond filling.
alentejo: In the Alentejo you turn old bread, garlic, coriander and olive oil into real meals. Cook an Açorda with poached egg, Carne de porco à alentejana with clams, or Migas, and bake a Pão alentejano to go with it.
berwar: The dishes from Berwar revolve around bulgur, lamb and homemade bread. You will find Pelpêç, chard rolls with rice and mince, Bamye, an okra and lamb stew, the thin Nanê sêlê flatbread, and even Savar, bulgur you make yourself.
main-dishes: What comes to the table in the evening ranges from venison medallions in juniper cream to Chikin Katsu with coleslaw. In between are aubergine and mince skewers, Sapporo Soup Curry and Rohrnudeln with vanilla sauce for those with a sweet tooth.
side-dishes: A good side often does more for a plate than the meat next to it. Here mashed potatoes, red cabbage with apple and homemade sauerkraut sit next to Irish Boxty and Takenoko Gohan, rice with bamboo shoots.
starters: A small plate is enough to begin with, such as Muhammara made from peppers and walnuts or baked Camembert with lingonberries. Salmon rolls with horseradish cream, Handkäs mit Musik or Maultaschen in broth work just as well.
soups: Clear broth or silky cream, a soup is easy to make ahead and often tastes rounder reheated. Here salsify cream soup sits next to Irish Colcannon Soup and Aşî Ebbas-Elî, a winter soup of wheat, beans and lentils.
salads: Salad here means more than leaves, it also means Bavarian sausage salad, meat salad and shrimp salad with egg. For something fresher there is fennel and pear salad, Panzanella with bread and tomatoes, or Japanese potato salad, Poteto Sarada.
breakfast: The day starts here with overnight oats, protein porridge or a Wicklow Pancake from the pan. If you prefer bread, you can put up preserves like pumpkin and orange or blackberry and apple, and redcurrant jelly for the pantry.
desserts: For dessert there are classics like Zwetschgenknödel (plum dumplings), Viennese apple strudel and chocolate pudding. Other kitchens bring Mango Sticky Rice, Portuguese Arroz doce with its cinnamon lattice, and Sericaia, an egg pudding with plums.
cakes: From Streuselkuchen on a tray to Rheinischer Prasselkuchen, you bake here what belongs with Sunday coffee. Alongside are Irish Porridge Bread, shortbread and Nanê birincî, Kurdish rice flour cookies with poppy seeds for Newroz.
baking: Baking here means Hefezopf (braided yeast loaf), Franzbrötchen and palmiers as much as Brown Scones and Rock Buns from Ireland. If you like working with dough, bake a Thuringian sour cream cake, a buckwheat torte or an Ulster Plain Loaf with its dark crust.
snacks: For in between there is something small to grab, like candied almonds, edamame or filled Onigiri. Heartier are cheese and ham muffins, Pão com chouriço with sausage baked in, or the Irish Crisp Sandwich, white bread with crisps.
drinks: A lot ends up in the glass here, from East Frisian tea and Genmaicha to the Kurdish mountain mint tea Çaya kakutî. For parties you mix peach punch, Kalte Ente or elderflower sparkling wine, and in winter there is eggnog and hot sea buckthorn.
basics: If you make your own stock, sauces and pastry, half the cooking is already done. Here you learn Shortcrust Pastry for pies, Tartare Sauce for fish, Sûzme from strained yoghurt and Lorik, a whey curd cheese.
casseroles: A bake is layered quickly, and the oven does the rest. Whether Pastitsio, a mince and pasta bake or fish and potato bake with mustard cream, everything goes into the dish, and it turns sweet with a plum and quark bake.
pasta: Pasta always works, whether plain as Spaghetti al Pomodoro or spicy as Penne all'Arrabbiata. For a bigger appetite there are spinach and ricotta cannelloni, gnocchi in sage butter and prawn linguine with chilli.
stews: Everything in one pot and let it braise, that is how Pichelsteiner, grandma's lentil stew and a classic beef goulash come together. If you like more spice, cook chili con carne, Hungarian paprika chicken or Sambar, a South Indian lentil stew.
pan-dishes: Fried potatoes with bacon, potato pancakes with apple sauce or gyoza you fold yourself all come out of the pan. For variety there is chicken piccata with lemon and capers, Mapo Tofu and Pad Krapao with Thai basil.
bowls: In a bowl everything sits side by side, rice or grains, vegetables, fish or meat and a sauce on top. That is how you build Korean Bibimbap, a teriyaki salmon bowl, a Buddha bowl with peanut sauce or the Vietnamese Bún bowl.
curries: A curry lives on spices that you toast in fat before the liquid goes in. India brings Palak Paneer, Chana Masala and Butter Chicken, Thailand the green curry with chicken.
vegetarian: Neither meat nor fish goes into the pot here, and you still eat well. Cook Bibimbap, Yasai-Ramen with vegetables or Kabocha no Nimono, braised pumpkin, and make a caramel pudding for dessert.
vegan: These recipes are labelled vegan, so without meat, fish, milk and eggs. What still ends up on the plate shows in Kinpira Gobo made from burdock root, Hevîrê sar with bulgur and herbs, the cauliflower shawarma wrap and a quince compote.
lactose-free: These recipes are labelled lactose-free. They include many Japanese dishes like Somen, Tsukune and Chanko-Nabe, as well as Potted Herrings from Ireland and Kurdish lamb dumplings. With ready-made ingredients it is still worth checking the label.
high-protein: The recipes here are labelled high in protein, and usually meat, fish or eggs are behind that. They range from Chikin Katsu to roast beef in one piece and scallops with bacon to a Steak and Mushroom Pie.
gluten-free: These recipes are labelled gluten-free. Beans, potatoes and eggs often carry the dishes, as in Favas com chouriço, Roast Potatoes or Pudim flan. With ready-made ingredients such as stock or soy sauce it is still worth checking the label.
low-carb: Recipes labelled low carb rely on meat, fish and vegetables rather than bread, pasta or rice. You will find duck breast, lamb skewers, cauliflower steaks and clams with garlic and coriander.
budget: On a small budget you can cook Açorda, the bread soup with poached egg, Arme Ritter (French toast), Boxty from potatoes or eggs in tomato and pepper sauce. Beans, yesterday's bread and a few eggs are often enough for a proper meal.
quick: For evenings with little time there is chicken piccata, wild garlic pesto pasta or a Greek village salad. Halve Hahn, the rye roll with cheese from the Rhineland, and sweet potato fries are also ready fast.
festive: For holidays and special evenings it can take a little more effort. Here you find Elisenlebkuchen and Spitzbuben for Advent, potato salad with sausages for Christmas Eve, red wine pears and a Thuringian Mutzbraten (smoked pork roast).
easy: These recipes get by with few steps and need no prior experience. Start with sausage goulash, apple crumble or banana bread, or cook Spanakorizo, the Greek spinach rice.
meal-prep: Cook on Sunday and only reheat during the week, that is what these recipes are for. Pichelsteiner stew, pulled pork, chicken and rice pot and overnight oats portion well and travel in a box.
air-fryer: The air fryer can do more than fries, as you can see from Quarkkeulchen, Hasselback potatoes and aubergine stacks with cheese. Onion rings, kohlrabi and turkey strips also turn crisp in it without a pot full of oil.
grilling: On the grill here go flank steak with chimichurri, Ćevapčići with ajvar and prawn skewers with garlic and paprika oil. If you skip meat, grill halloumi or vegetable skewers, and for dessert peaches with honey and yoghurt.
greek: Olive oil, lemon, oregano and sheep's cheese carry most of these dishes. Cook giouvetsi with orzo in a clay pot, roll dolmadakia in vine leaves, or bake galaktoboureko with semolina custard and lemon syrup to go with coffee.
turkish: Soups, börek, vegetables in olive oil and grilled meat sit side by side here. Start with mercimek çorbası, the red lentil soup, layer a su böreği with sheep's cheese, or make çılbır for breakfast: poached eggs on garlic yoghurt.
macedonia: Thessaloniki and the north give you bougatsa with semolina custard, trigona Panoramatos and mussels as mydia saganaki. There is also htipiti, the feta spread with roasted Florina peppers, and bouyiourdi, baked feta from the clay pot.
crete: Crete cooks with barley rusks, sheep's cream and plenty of olive oil. Make dakos with grated tomato and mizithra, braise lamb as tsigariasto, or bake kalitsounia, the sweet cheese tartlets with cinnamon and honey.
peloponnese: The Peloponnese brings Kalamata olives, oranges and syglino, the smoked pork. Try kagianas, scrambled eggs with tomato and feta, giant beans with syglino, or diples, folded pastry ribbons with honey and walnuts.
north-aegean: On Lesbos, Chios and Limnos people cook with fish, pulses and mastic. Here you will find kakavia, the fishermen's soup, squid stuffed with rice, flomaria pasta with braised rooster and sougania, stuffed onions.
cyclades: The Cyclades live on tomatoes, capers, yellow split peas and island cheese. Stir up fava Santorinis, fry ntomatokeftedes, the tomato fritters with mint, or bake a melopita with mizithra and honey.
ionian-islands: On Corfu, Kefalonia and Zakynthos you can taste the Venetian era: spices, tomato, vinegar and red wine. Cook pastitsada, rooster in a spiced sauce with thick pasta, sofrito with veal, or bourdeto, fish in a hot paprika sauce.
epirus: In Epirus people eat pita in every form, along with trout and mountain cheese. Roll out the filo yourself and bake hortopita with greens, kotopita with chicken, or alevropita, the crisp feta pie made from a pourable batter.
dodecanese: Rhodes, Symi and Karpathos bring chickpeas, honey, sesame and tiny shrimp to the kitchen. Make pitaroudia, the chickpea fritters from Rhodes, makarounes with caramelised onions, or melekouni, the sesame and honey bar.
thessaly: Thessaly cooks farmhouse food with sausage, peppers, trahanas and cheese. You get spetsofai from Pelion, trahanosoupa with feta, batzina, the thin courgette and cheese pie, and halvas Farsalon with almonds.
thrace: In Thrace, leeks, pork and walnuts are often on the table. Cook chirino prasoselino with leek and celery, fry kavourmas with eggs, or roll saragli, filo rolls with walnuts in syrup.
central-greece: Central Greece is largely about meat on the spit and fish on the grill. Make kontosouvli in the oven, arnaki vouloto in a sealed pot, or fry formaela, the cheese from Arachova.
attica: Attica and the islands off its coast mainly give you fish and sweets. Try psari spetsiota with a tomato crust, amygdalota from Hydra with rose water, or pasteli with pistachios from Aegina.
marmara: Istanbul, Bursa and Edirne supply palace cooking and street food alike. Cook çerkez tavuğu in walnut sauce, İskender kebap on bread with yoghurt, or midye pilaki, and for eating on the go there is balık ekmek with mackerel.
turkish-aegean: On the Aegean coast, fish, wild greens and vegetables in olive oil take centre stage. Grill octopus, wrap sardines in vine leaves, make fava from broad beans with dill, or çökertme kebabı on fried potatoes.
black-sea: On the Black Sea people eat anchovies, cornmeal, collard greens and butter. Here you will find hamsi buğulama, mıhlama with melted cheese, kara lahana sarması, and pide with minced or diced meat.
central-anatolia: Central Anatolia cooks with wheat, lamb and yoghurt. Make etli ekmek from Konya, keşkek from pounded wheat, tarhana çorbası, or cut erişte, egg noodles for drying.
turkish-mediterranean: From Antalya to Hatay the food turns hot, nutty and sweet. Shape Adana kebap onto skewers, stir up humus and babagannuş, and finish with künefe, shredded pastry with cheese in syrup.
southeastern-anatolia: Gaziantep and Urfa stand for kebab, bulgur and pistachios. Bake lahmacun, shape içli köfte, cook ezogelin çorbası with lentils and mint, or layer fıstıklı baklava.
eastern-anatolia: The east cooks hearty food with lamb, bulgur and apricots from Malatya. Try cağ kebabı from Erzurum, Harput köftesi in tomato sauce, piti from the little pot, or apricots with kaymak.
french: Butter, wine and patience shape this cuisine, from the bistro plate to the tart. Braise a Blanquette de veau, grate Carottes râpées as a quick starter, or layer a Charlotte aux fraises.
chinese: From steamed dim sum to fiery wok dishes, every province has its own cuisine. Start with Xihongshi Chao Jidan, scrambled eggs with tomato, fold Zhurou Baicai Jiaozi with pork and Chinese cabbage, or fry Yangzhou Chaofan from day-old rice.
spanish: Pan-cooked rice, salt cod, pulses and olive oil run through every region. Start with a Tortilla de patatas, cook a Paella valenciana over a wide flame, or put Patatas bravas and Gambas al ajillo on the table as tapas.
andalusia: Andalusia cooks light and cold against the heat, with almonds, sherry vinegar and plenty of fried seafood. Whisk up Ajoblanco malagueño with grapes, fry Berenjenas con miel de caña, or braise Atún encebollado in onions.
catalonia: Catalonia joins sea and mountains and seasons with nuts, garlic and roasted vegetables. Try Ànec amb peres, duck with pears, bake Bacallà a la llauna on the tray, or fry Botifarra amb mongetes with white beans.
galicia: Galicia lives on fish, potatoes and paprika oil. Cook Caldo gallego with turnip tops and white beans, put on a Caldeirada de pescado, or bake Bica de Trives, the sponge cake with a sugar crust.
valencia: In Valencia almost everything revolves around rice, whether pan-cooked, baked in the oven or coloured with ink. Cook Arroz al horno with chickpeas and ribs, Arroz negro with cuttlefish, or Arroz a banda, where the fish comes to the table separately.
basque-country: In the Basque Country, salt cod, peppers and olive oil make some of the finest sauces in Spain. Stir Bacalao al pil pil until the sauce binds, braise Chipirones en su tinta, or skewer a Gilda of olive, anchovy and pickled pepper.
madrid: Madrid eats hearty and loves a snack in between. Get yourself Churros con chocolate for breakfast, fill a Bocadillo de calamares with fried squid rings, or slide Besugo al horno a la madrileña into the oven.
murcia: Murcia cooks with vegetables from the huerta, rice and dried ñora peppers. Try Arroz caldero with allioli, Arroz con conejo with rosemary, or Conejo al ajo cabañil in garlic and vinegar.
asturias: Asturias stands for cider, strong cheese and big portions. Fry a Cachopo of two veal cutlets with ham and cheese, bake Bollos preñaos with chorizo, or stir Arroz con leche asturiano with a caramelised sugar crust.
balearic-islands: In the Balearic Islands fish, vegetables and lard pastries come together. Bake an Ensaïmada, top a Coca de trampó with pepper and tomato, or cook Arròs brut, the spicy rice pot with chicken and pork.
castile-and-leon: Castile and León is the land of wood-oven roasts and chickpeas. Slide Cochinillo asado into the oven, eat Cocido maragato in reverse order, or bake Hornazo de Salamanca, the filled pastry pie.
cantabria: Cantabria cooks with anchovies, tuna and mountain beans. Make Bonito con tomate, braise Bocartes a la cazuela in a clay pot, or put on Cocido lebaniego with chickpeas.
canary-islands: The Canaries season with mojo, gofio and plenty of garlic. Cook Papas arrugadas con mojo in salted water, marinate Conejo en salmorejo, or whisk Bienmesabe, the almond cream with egg yolk and lemon.
aragon: Aragon cooks simply, with vegetables from the Ebro, lamb and almonds. Try Borrajas con patatas, braise Magras con tomate, or make Guirlache, the almond brittle with aniseed.
castilla-la-mancha: La Mancha is shepherd's cooking with garlic, paprika and game. Fry Duelos y quebrantos of egg, chorizo and bacon, roast Asadillo manchego in the oven, or preserve Lomo de orza in olive oil.
navarre: Navarre is known for its vegetables, from white asparagus to the lettuce hearts of Tudela. Braise Cordero al chilindrón in pepper and tomato, make a Menestra de verduras, or Bacalao al ajoarriero.
extremadura: Extremadura cooks with Pimentón de la Vera, lamb and Iberian pork. Fry Migas extremeñas of breadcrumbs and chorizo, braise Caldereta extremeña de cordero, or mix Zorongollo of roasted peppers.
la-rioja: La Rioja cooks to go with wine, with chorizo, paprika and vine-cutting embers. Make Patatas a la riojana, cook red beans as Caparrones, or grill Chuletillas al sarmiento.
guangdong: Cantonese cooking is mild and fresh and lives on steaming and short cooking. Make Bai Qie Ji with ginger and spring onion sauce, steam Char Siu Bao, or cook Bao Zai Fan, clay pot rice with sausage and chicken.
shanghai-zhejiang: Around Shanghai much of the food tastes slightly sweet and is slowly braised in soy sauce. Braise Dongpo Rou, toss Cong You Ban Mian with spring onion oil, or steam Babao Fan, the sticky rice with eight treasures.
sichuan-chongqing: Sichuan seasons with chilli and Sichuan pepper, which lightly numbs the tongue. Cook Chongqing Xiao Mian, fry Ganbian Sijidou, the dry-fried green beans, or braise Doubanyu in chilli bean paste.
northwest-china: In the northwest people eat wheat noodles and lamb with cumin. Pull Youpo Biangbiang Mian, cook Lanzhou Niurou Lamian in clear beef broth, or fry Ziran Yangrou in the wok.
hong-kong-macau: Hong Kong and Macau mix Cantonese cooking with influences from Europe. Bake Boluo Bao, the pineapple buns, gratinate Ju Zhupa Fan with pork chop and tomato sauce, or cook Minchi, minced meat with potatoes from Macau.
beijing: Beijing eats robustly, with lamb, wheat and sweet bean sauce. Fry Jingjiang Rousi, put Shuan Yangrou on the table as a hot pot, or pull Tanghulu, candied fruit on a skewer.
jiangsu: Jiangsu stands for fine knife work and clear, mild broths. Fry Yangzhou Chaofan, cook Yangchun Mian as a plain noodle soup, or try Wensi Doufu Geng with hair-fine sliced tofu.
dongbei: The northeast cooks hearty for cold winters, with sauerkraut, potatoes and braising pots. Fry Di San Xian of aubergine, potato and pepper, braise Xiaoji Dun Mogu with mushrooms and glass noodles, or toss Laohu Cai, the tiger salad.
shandong: Shandong is considered the cradle of northern Chinese cooking, with vinegar, leeks and plenty of heat in the wok. Fry Culiu Baicai, braise Guota Doufu in an egg coating, or pull sugar threads for Basi Digua.
henan-hubei: Between the Yellow River and the Yangtze people eat soups, flatbreads and lotus root. Cook Hulatang, the pepper soup, fill Jidan Guanbing with egg, or put on Lianou Paigu Tang with pork ribs.
hunan: Hunan cooks hot and sour, with fresh and pickled chillies. Steam Duojiao Zhengyu, fry Nongjia Xiaochao Rou with green chillies, or make Dong'an Ji with vinegar.
yunnan-guizhou: In the southwest much of the food tastes sour and spicy, with herbs and rice noodles. Try Guoqiao Mixian, the cross-the-bridge noodles, or Suantang Feiniu, beef in sour broth.
shanxi: Shanxi is the land of noodles and dark vinegar. Roll Cuo Yu, shape Mao Er Duo, the cat's ear noodles, or steam Youmian Kaolaolao from oat flour.
fujian: Fujian cooks with fish, clear broths and a slightly sweet note. Cook Fuzhou Yu Wan Tang with filled fish balls, or make Rousong, the fluffy meat floss.
guangxi-hainan: The deep south eats rice noodles, coconut and tropical fruit. Start with Guilin Mifen, rice noodles with braised meat.
anhui: Anhui cooks with mountain herbs, bamboo and ham. Try Huangshan Shaobing, crisp flatbreads with dried vegetables.
paris: Paris is bistro and bakery in one. Bake a Baguette, braise Bœuf à la mode with carrots, or make Céleri rémoulade as a starter.
provence: Provence cooks with olive oil, garlic, anchovies and herbs. Put on a Bouillabaisse, braise Daube provençale with orange and olives, or whisk Anchoïade as a dip.
loire-valley: In the Loire Valley people eat light, with river fish, asparagus and white wine. Make Fricassée de poulet à l'angevine, whisk Crémet d'Anjou, or bake Gâteau nantais with almonds and rum.
brittany: Brittany lives on salted butter, buckwheat and seafood. Bake a Galette complète with ham, cheese and egg, cook Cotriade, the fish stew, or slide Far breton with prunes into the oven.
languedoc-roussillon: Between the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean, beans, salt cod and Catalan influences meet. Put on a Cassoulet, whisk Brandade de morue, or roast vegetables for Escalivade.
nord-picardy: The north cooks with beer, chicory and leeks. Braise Carbonade flamande, gratinate Endives au jambon, or bake a Flamiche aux poireaux.
auvergne-limousin: The Massif Central is cheese and potato country. Stir Aligot until it stretches in strands, stuff a Chou farci, or bake Clafoutis aux cerises.
lyon-dauphine: Lyon is considered the capital of French home cooking, while the Dauphiné supplies walnuts and gratin. Slide a Gratin dauphinois into the oven, stir Cervelle de canut, or bake Bugnes lyonnaises.
poitou-charentes: On the Atlantic coast people eat oysters, fish and butter cake. Cook Chaudrée charentaise, braise Lapin au pineau, or break a Broyé du Poitou into pieces.
southwest-france: The southwest is duck country, with porcini and red wine from Bordeaux. Cook Confit de canard in its own fat, make Garbure of cabbage and beans, or bake Canelés.
corsica: Corsica cooks with chestnut flour, Brocciu and wild herbs. Bake Fiadone, the fresh cheese cake, fill Bastelle with chard, or fry an Omelette au brocciu et à la menthe.
savoy: In Savoy cheese warms you through the winter. Make Croûte au fromage savoyarde with Reblochon, cook Diots au vin blanc, or bake Gâteau de Savoie.
burgundy: Burgundy cooks with its wine and with mustard from Dijon. Braise Bœuf bourguignon or Coq au vin and bake Gougères, the cheese puffs, to go with it.
normandy: Normandy relies on cream, apples and cider. Braise Poulet vallée d'Auge with Calvados, cook Moules à la normande, or roast a Camembert rôti in its wooden box.
alsace: Alsace joins French and German cooking. Layer a Baeckeoffe, cook Choucroute garnie with sausages, or bake a Kougelhopf.
franche-comte: Franche-Comté cooks with Comté, morels and Vin jaune. Make Poulet au vin jaune et aux morilles, melt a Mont-d'Or chaud in the oven, or toast Croûte aux morilles.
french-basque-country: In the French Basque Country Piment d'Espelette seasons almost everything. Braise Axoa of veal, cook Poulet basquaise with peppers and tomatoes, or bake a Gâteau basque.
champagne: Champagne cooks down to earth and sometimes with its wine. Put on Potée champenoise, braise Poularde au champagne, or bake Biscuits roses de Reims.
lorraine: Lorraine is the home of quiche and mirabelle plums. Bake a Quiche lorraine, a Tarte aux mirabelles, or Madeleines from Commercy.
